title: Wall Street Is Rushing to Fund the AI Bonanza in Every Conceivable Way

vocab.articleQuote: Wall Street Is Rushing to Fund the AI Bonanza in Every Conceivable Way.
vocab.inContext: Here the AI build-out is treated as a giant money-making opportunity — a flood of profit and investment that everyone wants a piece of.
vocab.meaning: A sudden source of great wealth or good luck; a situation that produces a lot of something valuable all at once.
examples: The bake sale turned into a bonanza when a local bakery donated a hundred cupcakes and everything sold out in an hour.
Opening that booster pack was a bonanza — three rare cards in a row.

vocab.articleQuote: Still, demand from investors has generally defied the skeptics so far.
vocab.inContext: Investors kept eagerly buying AI-related stocks and bonds even though doubters predicted the enthusiasm would fade — the demand went against those predictions.
vocab.meaning: To openly resist or refuse to obey; or, when you say something "defies" expectations, to go against what people predicted.
examples: Even though everyone expected the underdog team to lose, they defied the odds and won the championship.
She defied her coach's prediction by shaving ten seconds off her best time.

vocab.articleQuote: But the daunting expenses pushed all of the hyperscalers but Microsoft to the bond market last year.
vocab.inContext: The costs of building AI data centers were so huge and intimidating that companies couldn't cover them with their own cash and had to borrow.
vocab.meaning: Seeming so large, difficult, or intimidating that it discourages you or makes you nervous to face it.
examples: Starting high school in a brand-new town felt daunting until she made her first friend.
The summer reading list looked daunting at first, but it turned out to be only five short books.

concepts.name: Raising money: equity vs. debt
concepts.articleQuote: The casual announcement of an $85 billion equity raise.
concepts.inContext: Alphabet (Google's parent) chose to raise $85 billion by selling new shares — an "equity raise" — while other tech giants raised cash by issuing bonds. The article's point is that companies are using every method at once.
concepts.meaning: A company that needs cash has two basic options. With equity it sells slices of ownership (shares): it never has to pay the money back, but the new owners now share in future profits. With debt (like bonds) it borrows money it must repay later with interest, but the lenders get no ownership. Tech firms funding AI are doing both — selling shares and borrowing — on a massive scale.

concepts.name: AI hyperscalers
concepts.articleQuote: the AI hyperscalers Alphabet, Amazon.com, Meta Platforms, Microsoft and Oracle have issued $159 billion of bonds globally this year.
concepts.inContext: These are the handful of giant companies building the enormous data centers that power AI, and they're borrowing huge sums to do it.
concepts.meaning: A hyperscaler is a company that runs computing at "hyper" scale — gigantic data centers full of servers and chips that it rents out as cloud computing. Because AI models need vast amounts of computing power, these few companies are spending and borrowing enormous amounts to build that infrastructure.

concepts.name: Shareholder dilution
concepts.articleQuote: increased equity issuance could pressure stocks by diluting shareholders—one possible factor behind last week's tech selloff.
concepts.inContext: When a company like Alphabet issues lots of new shares to raise cash, the people who already own shares suddenly own a smaller fraction of the company — which can push the stock price down.
concepts.meaning: Imagine a pizza cut into 8 slices and you own 1. If the company suddenly cuts it into 16 slices, your slice is smaller even though you still hold one piece. Issuing new shares does the same to ownership: each existing share becomes a smaller piece of the company and of its future profits. That "watering down" is called dilution, and it's one reason a big share sale can make a stock fall.

concepts.name: Bond spreads over Treasurys
concepts.articleQuote: The extra return that investors get for holding U.S. companies' bonds instead of ultrasafe Treasurys is hovering near multidecade lows.
concepts.inContext: Investors are demanding only a tiny bit of extra interest to lend to tech companies rather than to the U.S. government — a sign they feel very safe doing it, despite the AI risks.
concepts.meaning: U.S. government bonds (Treasurys) are treated as the safest place to lend money. Any riskier borrower has to pay a little more interest to attract lenders; that extra amount is the "spread." A wide spread means investors see lots of risk; a narrow spread — near record lows here — means they feel confident the borrower will pay them back.

concepts.name: Investment-grade vs. speculative-grade bonds
concepts.articleQuote: Though rated investment-grade, its bonds trade more in line with the highest tier of speculative-grade debt.
concepts.inContext: Rating agencies officially call Oracle's debt fairly safe (investment-grade), but investors are treating it as riskier — pricing it like the safest end of "junk" — because Oracle is expected to burn through tens of billions building its cloud business.
concepts.meaning: Independent agencies grade a borrower's bonds by how likely the borrower is to pay them back. "Investment-grade" means a low risk of default; "speculative-grade" (also called high-yield or "junk") means higher risk — so those borrowers must pay higher interest. The grade is only an opinion, so the market can sometimes treat a bond as riskier or safer than its official rating.

quiz.question: According to the article, why are tech companies raising such enormous amounts of money right now?
options: To pay larger dividends to their shareholders
To fund the build-out of AI data centers and infrastructure
To buy back their own stock from the market
To repay debts left over from the 1850s railroad boom
quiz.explanation: The article says tech companies are "hungry for cash to invest in data centers" to power the AI build-out.

quiz.question: Alphabet announced an $85 billion equity raise. Why can selling lots of new shares push a company's stock price down?
options: The company must immediately repay all the new money with interest
An equity raise automatically triggers a recession
New shares dilute existing shareholders, so each share becomes a smaller piece of the company
It legally forces the company to stop selling products
quiz.explanation: Issuing new shares spreads ownership across more shares — dilution — so each existing share is worth a smaller slice of the company and its profits.

quiz.question: What is an "AI hyperscaler," as the article uses the term?
options: A government agency that regulates artificial intelligence
A type of high-speed undersea internet cable
A giant tech company that runs massive data centers and cloud computing
A startup that has never earned any revenue
quiz.explanation: Hyperscalers like Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Microsoft and Oracle operate cloud computing at enormous scale and are building the data centers behind AI.

quiz.question: The article notes that Oracle's bonds are "rated investment-grade" but "trade more in line with... speculative-grade debt." What does that suggest?
options: Investors treat Oracle's debt as riskier than its official rating implies
Oracle has stopped paying interest on its bonds
Oracle's bonds are now the safest in the entire market
Oracle is no longer legally allowed to borrow money
quiz.explanation: Even though rating agencies call the debt investment-grade, the market prices it like riskier speculative-grade ("junk") debt, because Oracle is expected to burn through cash.

quiz.question: "Demand from investors has generally defied the skeptics so far." In this sentence, "defied" most nearly means—
options: obeyed without question
explained in careful detail
copied exactly
went against and proved wrong
quiz.explanation: To defy expectations is to go against them — investor demand stayed strong even though skeptics predicted it would fade.
